In 1961, the Indian National Committee for Space Research (NCSR) launched India's first research rocket from the Thumba Equatorial Launch Center in Thumba in the State of Kerala. In 1967, our indigenously built rocket Rohini-75 was successfully launched. The next stage was the successful launch of the first Indian satellite Aryabhatta in 1975 with help from the Soviet Russia, and this success proved that Indian scientists can indigenously build and launch a satellite. After the success of this basic programme in space research and rockets, the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) was established on 15th August 1969 to carry out further space research, with its headquarters at Bengaluru. ISRO activated the space station at Sriharikota in Andhra Pradesh for launching our satellites in space.

The Department of Telecommunications under the Ministry of Communications started the telex service in 1963. Its purpose was to transmit typed messages from one part of the country to another rapidly. In 1969, the telex service started in Devanagari script in Delhi and later it spread all over the country. This service began to be used in different fields. With the rise of the internet after 1990, the significance of this service reduced.

India successfully performed her first nuclear test at Pokharan in Rajasthan on 18th May 1974. The test was in consonance with the policy of using nuclear energy for peaceful purposes and for self-sufficiency. The reason why India took this decision was China's nuclear capability and Pakistan's desperate efforts to acquire nuclear weapons with China's help. Prime Minister Indira Gandhi took the decision of carrying out this 'nuclear explosion', and Dr Homi Sethna, the chairman of the Indian Atomic Energy Commission, and Dr Raja Ramanna, Director of the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, played a major role in conducting it. Pokharan was chosen on the basis of the required criteria for the location of nuclear tests, that is, it was far away from human settlement and had no ground water reserves. After this test the U.S.A. refused to give India the technology for defence related fields such as space research, communications and missile development, and so India adopted a policy of developing its own missile development programme.

Bhaskar-1 was a remote sensing experimental satellite which India launched from the Soviet Russia in 1979. It was launched in order to observe various things on the surface of the earth by remote sensing technology. This remote sensing technology was useful for India's development in regard to water bodies, mineral deposits and forecasting weather, and the photographs taken with its help about the bowels of the earth, the environment and forests were important. Another area in which the information from this satellite was useful was oceanography. In 1981, 'Bhaskar-2' was launched from Soviet Russia.

India's first Prime Minister Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru wanted to nurture a scientific temper and to bring about the nation's progress, and it was from this perspective that he set up the Indian Atomic Energy Commission on 10th August 1948. Dr Homi Bhabha was appointed as the first Chairman of the Commission. The objectives of the Commission were to produce electricity from atomic energy, to increase the yield of food grains and make them last longer, to set up the technology for achieving this and to develop nanotechnology. Working in this direction, the Department of Atomic Energy set up 'Apsara', a nuclear reactor functioning on atomic energy, in 1956, and an atomic power station was set up at Tarapur in 1969. Thus the Commission was established so that atomic energy could be used for the development of the country.

India performed her first nuclear test at Pokharan in Rajasthan on 18th May 1974 in consonance with the policy of using nuclear energy for peaceful purposes and for self-sufficiency. The reason why India took this decision was China's nuclear capability and Pakistan's desperate efforts to acquire nuclear weapons with China's help. In such a situation India had to think of its own security. Later, on 11th May 1998, India carried out its second nuclear test to prove its nuclear preparedness, and three tests were done on that day, one of them being of the Hydrogen Bomb. At the same time Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee assured that there would be no first use of nuclear weapons by India.

On 11th May 1998, India carried out its second nuclear test to prove its nuclear preparedness. Three tests were done on this day and one of them was of the Hydrogen Bomb. Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee assured that there would be no first use of nuclear weapons by India. Even so, the USA did not accept India's nuclear preparedness and it imposed economic sanctions on India immediately after these tests. The USA had behaved in a similar way earlier also, because after India's first nuclear test at Pokharan in 1974 it had refused to give India the technology for defence related fields such as space research, communications and missile development.

Satellite technology has influenced many services that people use in everyday life.

In August 1983, the satellite INSAT 1-B was launched in space and because of this satellite a major revolution came about in the areas of telecommunication, television, radio, weather forecasting and space research in India. Due to INSAT, 207 Akashwani or Radio stations could be connected to each other. This mechanism was also useful for the search and rescue of people caught in some disaster like a shipwreck or an air plane crash, for forecasting weather, and to look for and follow cyclones or storms. It was useful in the fields of telemedicine and educational institutions as well. The telemedicine service enabled the population from remote areas to get advice and treatment from expert doctors, and Public Primary Health Centers in villages have been connected with superspecialty hospitals through INSAT.

The remote sensing satellite Bhaskar-1, launched in 1979, helped in observing various things on the surface of the earth. This technology was useful in regard to water bodies, mineral deposits and forecasting weather, and also in oceanography, and the photographs taken with its help about the bowels of the earth, the environment and forests were important.

The satellite APPLE, launched on 19th June 1981, was beneficial in the field of education and its objective of providing emergency telecommunication services was successful. In this way satellite technology has reached the ordinary people through the telephone, television, radio, weather reports, disaster rescue, medical advice and education that they use every day.

Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam is known as the father of India's missile programme and he is also referred to as the 'Missile Man' of India.

In 1958, the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) was established under the Department of Defence of the government of India. The objective of this organisation was to make India self-sufficient with respect to the means, equipment and weapons required for defence. After 1983, this organisation developed several missiles under the leadership of Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, and he made a great contribution in the production of missiles.

The Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme (IGMDP) was conceived by Dr Kalam and was carried out under his leadership, while the task of building the missiles was undertaken by DRDO. Under this programme India successfully tested the missile Prithvi in 1988 and the missile Agni in 1989, and the entire world took note of India's programme of developing nuclear missiles indigenously. The missile Akash, which fires from land into air, was developed in 1990, and the missile Nag was made in order to destroy the tanks of the enemy. India has militarily become secure due to the production of these missiles. Because of this great contribution to India's missiles, Dr Kalam is called the 'Missile Man'.

The reservation of seats for rail travel used to be done by hand earlier. In order to bring efficiency, accuracy and coordination in the reservation system in rail travel, the computerised reservation system was started for the first time in Delhi in 1984. In the same year, the Metro was started in Kolkata. The chapter mentions this computerised reservation system as one of the examples of the technology adopted by the railways, and it says that the technology adopted by railways has a big role in the history of modern India.

The Konkan Railway started in 1998 and there are several records of technology to its credit.

This railway stretches over the four States of Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka and Kerala, over a distance of 760 kilometres. There are 92 tunnels on this track and the 6.5 km tunnel at Karbude is the longest among them. There are 179 big bridges and 1819 small bridges on this track. Out of these, the 2065.8 m long bridge on the River Sharavati near Honnawar is the biggest, while the 64 m tall bridge on the River Panval near Ratnagiri is India's tallest bridge. Some parts of this track are prone to landslides, so for avoiding accidents there are sensors fitted to the railway engines. E. Sreedharan, who is famous by the nickname 'Metroman', did noteworthy work regarding the Konkan Railway.
